l: Ariadne, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Ariadne is shown sitting on a rock near Ocnus and looking at her sister Phædra, who hangs from a rock by a rope. Dionysus is said to have taken Ariadne from Theseus, either by chance or through a deliberate ambush.

l: Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Dionysus is said to have taken Ariadne from Theseus, possibly by sailing against him with a larger armament. He is also identified as the Dionysus who first invaded India and built a bridge over the Euphrates at a place called Zeugma.

l: Theseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Theseus is seated with Pirithous on an enchanted rock, holding both his own sword and Pirithous’ sword. Panyasis says that the rock grew to them instead of fetters, and Homer is cited as praising the friendship between Theseus and Pirithous.

l: Pirithous, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Pirithous is seated with Theseus on the enchanted rock and looks at his sword as if indignant that swords are useless for their present venture. His friendship with Theseus is praised in passages from Homer.

l: picture (Polygnotus’ painting), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The picture shows Ocnus making rope, Ariadne watching Phædra, Odysseus performing a rite beside a ditch, and Theseus and Pirithous seated on an enchanted rock. It also includes numerous other mythological figures, including Perimedes, Eurylochus, Tityus, Chloris, Thyia, Procris, Clymene, Megara, Eriphyle, Elpenor, Tiresias, and Anticlea.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Polygnotus depicts the daughters of Pandareus, several Trojan-war figures, and other mythic characters in a painted scene. The daughters, Camiro and Clytie, are shown crowned with flowers and playing with dice, while Pandareus is identified as a Milesian associated with Tantalus in theft and perjury. Phocus and Iaseus are portrayed recalling their friendship through a signet-ring, although Peleus later contrived Phocus’ death. The painting also includes Actæon, Orpheus, Thamyris, Marsyas, and others, with details indicating their stories, attributes, or fates.

l: Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Polygnotus painted the daughters of Pandareus, Phocus, Iaseus, Actæon, Orpheus, Thamyris, Marsyas, and many other figures in the scene. He depicted Orpheus in Greek dress beside a willow, Thamyris blind and dejected with a broken lyre, and Marsyas seated near Olympus, who is learning to play the pipe.

l: daughters of Pandareus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The daughters of Pandareus were Camiro and Clytie. Their parents died through the wrath of the gods while they were maidens; Aphrodite raised them, and other goddesses gave them gifts, but the Harpies carried them off and gave them to the Furies. Polygnotus painted them crowned with flowers and playing with dice.

l: Pandareus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Pandareus was a Milesian from Cretan Miletus and an associate of Tantalus in theft and perjury. He was the father of Camiro and Clytie.

l: Phocus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Phocus, the son of Æacus, crossed from Ægina to the mainland region later called Phocis, obtained sovereignty there, and intended to live there. Iaseus was his friend and gave him various presents, including a gold-set stone signet-ring; when Phocus later sailed back to Ægina, Peleus contrived his death. Polygnotus depicted Phocus as a stripling allowing Iaseus to take the ring from his left hand.

l: Iaseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Iaseus was very friendly with Phocus and offered him various gifts, including a stone signet-ring set in gold. In Polygnotus’ painting, he is shown trying to take the ring from Phocus’ left hand as a memorial of their friendship.

l: Actæon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Actæon, the son of Aristæus, is depicted seated with his mother on a deerskin and holding a fawn. A hunting hound is nearby, serving as an emblem of Actæon’s life and death.

l: Orpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Orpheus is depicted sitting on a hill in what appears to be the grove of Proserpine, touching the branches of a willow-tree while holding a harp. His dress is Greek rather than Thracian, and he is shown with a hat that is not Thracian.

l: Thamyris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Thamyris is depicted sitting near Pelias, blind and dejected, with thick hair and beard. His lyre is broken and its strings have been torn apart.

l: Marsyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Marsyas is depicted seated on a stone near Olympus, a handsome boy who is learning to play the pipe. The Phrygians at Celænæ say that the river flowing through their town was formerly Marsyas, that he invented piping in honour of Cybele, and that he helped them repulse the Galatian army with the river’s water and his melody.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The painting depicts numerous mythological figures, including enemies of Odysseus, the mournful Hector, Memnon and Sarpedon, Paris and Penthesilea, and figures suffering punishments. Polygnotus portrays Ajax the son of Oileus as shipwrecked, Meleager looking toward him, and several scenes associated with death, mourning, and the underworld. The painting also includes Callisto, Nomia, Pero, Sisyphus, people parodying or appearing to mock the Eleusinian mysteries, and Tantalus enduring punishments described by Homer and Archilochus.

l: the painting, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The painting contains scenes and figures from several myths, including Actæon, the two Ajaxes, Palamedes, Thersites, Meleager, Hector, Memnon, Sarpedon, Paris, Penthesilea, Callisto, Sisyphus, and Tantalus. It also shows people carrying water, a winejar, birds on Memnon’s cloak, and figures apparently making a mock of the Eleusinian mysteries.

l: Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Polygnotus painted the scene and seems to have deliberately gathered together enemies of Odysseus. He followed the account of Archilochus in depicting Tantalus, though it is uncertain whether Archilochus invented the additional detail of the overhanging stone.

l: Palamedes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Palamedes is shown playing dice with Actæon, Salaminian Ajax, and Thersites; the text says that he invented dice. The Cyprian Poems state that Diomede and Odysseus drowned him while he was fishing, and he is the only one of this group without a beard.

l: Ajax the son of Oileus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Ajax the son of Oileus is shown looking at the others playing dice, with the appearance of a shipwrecked man and a body wet with sea foam. He hated Odysseus because Odysseus urged the Greeks to stone him for his rape of Cassandra.

l: Odysseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Odysseus is presented as an enemy of Ajax the son of Oileus. He urged the Greeks to stone Ajax for his rape of Cassandra, and the Cyprian Poems say that he helped Diomede drown Palamedes.

l: Meleager, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Meleager is painted slightly above Ajax the son of Oileus, looking at him. Homer attributes his death to a Fury hearing Althæa curse him, while the Great Eœæ and the Minyad say that Apollo killed him while assisting the Curetes against the Ætolians.

l: Hector, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Hector is seated in the lower part of the painting near Thracian Thamyris, appearing oppressed with sorrow and holding both hands on his left knee.

l: Memnon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Memnon is seated on a stone beside Hector and near Sarpedon, with one hand on Sarpedon’s shoulder. Birds called Memnonides are painted on his cloak; according to local belief, they annually visit his tomb near the Hellespont and clear and sprinkle the area around it. Memnon was king of the Ethiopians, but the text says he came to Ilium from Susa in Persia and the river Choaspes.

l: Sarpedon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Sarpedon is shown beside Memnon, leaning his head on both hands while one of Memnon’s hands rests on his shoulder.

l: Paris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Paris is depicted above Sarpedon and Memnon as a beardless youth. He claps his hands like a rustic, apparently trying to attract Penthesilea’s attention.

l: Penthesilea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Penthesilea looks at Paris but appears to despise and jeer at him as a boy. She is represented as a maiden carrying a Scythian bow and wearing a leopard’s skin around her shoulders.

l: Callisto, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Callisto, the daughter of Lycaon, is shown with a bear-skin coverlet and her feet resting on the knees of Nomia.

l: Sisyphus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Sisyphus, the son of Æolus, is shown laboriously rolling a stone up a hill.

l: the Eleusinian Mysteries, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The painting includes figures who may be people making a mock of the Eleusinian mysteries, although this is only a conjecture. The older Greeks regarded those mysteries as greatly superior to all other religious services.

l: Tantalus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Tantalus is depicted under the winejar undergoing the punishments described by Homer. He is also terrified that a stone overhanging his head will fall on him.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Delphi has a handsome theatre, a statue of Dionysus offered by the men of Cnidos, and a stadium made of Mount Parnassus stone that Herodes later embellished with Pentelican marble. The Corycian cavern on Mount Parnassus is sacred to Pan and the Corycian Nymphs, and is described as especially accessible and remarkable, with springs and water dripping from its roof. Tithorea contains the remains of a theatre and market-place, a grove and shrine of Athene, and the tomb of Antiope and Phocus. Near Tithorea is a highly sacred shrine of Isis, where access is granted only to those invited by Isis in dreams and where the Festival of Isis is held twice yearly.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Delphi has a handsome theatre near its temple precincts, a statue of Dionysus offered by the men of Cnidos, and a stadium in the highest part of the city. The stadium was originally made of Mount Parnassus stone and was later embellished with Pentelican marble by the Athenian Herodes.

l: Parnassus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Mount Parnassus is about 60 stades from Delphi by the road leading toward it, and the Corycian cavern lies on its slopes. Its heights are higher than the clouds, and the Thyiades conduct their mad revels there in honour of Dionysus and Apollo.

l: Corycian cavern, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: The Corycian cavern is named after the Nymph Corycia and is considered more remarkable than the other caverns described. Much of it can be traversed without torches; it has a high roof, springs, and water dripping from the roof, and the people of Mount Parnassus consider it sacred to Pan and the Corycian Nymphs.

l: Tithorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Tithorea is about 80 stades from Delphi by way of Mount Parnassus, though a less mountainous carriage road is longer. It contains the remains of a theatre and ancient market-place, a grove and shrine of Athene, and the tomb of Antiope and Phocus; the river Cachales supplies its inhabitants with water. The people say that its name comes from the Nymph Tithorea, and that its fortunes worsened a generation before the account.

l: shrine of Isis near Tithorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: The shrine of Isis is about 40 stades from the temple of Æsculapius and is described as the holiest of the Greek shrines to the Egyptian goddess. The people of Tithorea do not live near it, and no one may approach unless Isis has first invited that person in dreams.

l: Isis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Isis is worshipped at the shrine near Tithorea, where she determines whom to admit by inviting them in dreams. Her worship there includes twice-yearly festivals and sacrifices of animals other than swine, sheep, and goats.

l: Festival of Isis at Tithorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: The Festival of Isis is celebrated twice each year, in Spring and Autumn. Before each festival the shrine is secretly purified and remains from the previous sacrifices are buried; traders then set up tents, sell slaves, animals, clothing, silver, and gold, and the sacrifice is held at noon. The victims are wrapped in linen or flax, carried in a solemn procession, and burned in or before the shrine, after which the tents are burned and the participants depart quickly.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: The text describes roads and settlements in Phocis, including Ledon, Lilæa, Charadra, Parapotamii, Amphiclea, Tithronium, and Drymæa. Ledon was deserted because of its weakness, while Lilæa was restored after expelling a Macedonian garrison and contained temples, a theatre, a market-place, and baths. Charadra depended on a stream for water, and the fertile land near the Cephisus was divided mainly into farms. Amphiclea was associated with traditions about a protective snake and with Dionysian prophecy and healing, while Drymæa contained an ancient temple to Law-giving Demeter.

l: Tithorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Tithorea is the starting point of a road leading to Ledon. Another route from Tithorea leads toward Drymæa through Tithronium.

l: Ledon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Ledon was formerly considered a town, but in the author's time it had been deserted by its inhabitants because of its weakness. About 80 inhabitants lived near the Cephisus and called their settlement Ledon; the former town was said to have received its name from an Autochthon named Ledon, and its destruction was attributed to the impiety of Philomelus.

l: Cephisus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: The settlement called Ledon stood near the Cephisus, 40 stades from the ruins of the former town. The Cephisus rises at Lilæa and initially flows with such force that, especially at midday, it roars like a bull; the land near it is described as the best in Phocis for planting, sowing, and pasture.

l: Lilæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Lilæa is a winter day's journey from Delphi and about 60 stades from Amphiclea. After being restored, it was besieged by Philip the son of Demetrius, but Patron led the younger citizens against the Macedonian garrison and forced it to leave; Lilæa honored Patron with a statue at Delphi. The town had a theatre, market-place, baths, and temples to Apollo and Artemis, and was said to be named after Lilæa, one of the Naiades and a daughter of the Cephisus.

l: Charadra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Charadra lies about 20 stades beyond Lilæa on a lofty ridge. Its inhabitants had little water, relying on the Charadrus, a stream three stades down the hillside that flows into the Cephisus; the market-place contained altars to Heroes, identified by some as Castor and Pollux and by others as local heroes.

l: Parapotamii, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Parapotamii was one of the Phocian towns burned by Xerxes. It was not restored by the Athenians and Bœotians, and its inhabitants were distributed among other towns because of its poverty and lack of money; no ruins remained and its exact site was unknown.

l: Amphiclea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Amphiclea lies 60 stades from Lilæa, and its name differed from the Amphicæa used by Herodotus and the Amphiclea used by the Amphictyones. Its inhabitants associated the place with a story in which a snake protected a child and was accidentally killed with him, and they also performed secret orgies to Dionysus, who was believed to give prophecies and cure sickness through dreams.

l: Drymæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Drymæa lies about 20 stades beyond Tithronium and about 80 stades from Amphiclea according to Herodotus. It was originally called Nauboles and was said to have been founded by Phocus the son of Æacus; it contained an ancient temple to Law-giving Demeter, whose erect stone statue was honored at an annual Thesmophoria.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Elatea is described as a major town of Phocis that resisted Cassander and the Macedonians, was subdued by the Romans under Titus Flaminius, and later earned freedom and immunity from taxation by resisting Taxilus and the barbarians from Pontus. Its traditions connect its foundation with Elatus, son of Areas, and its monuments include a market-place, a statue of Elatus, a temple of Æsculapius, a theatre, and an ancient bronze statue of Athene. During the invasion of the Costoboci, Mnesibulus led Elatean defenders against them and was killed after slaying many barbarians. Near Elatea stands the temple of Athene Cranæa, whose priest served for five years and whose armed statue was made by the sons of Polycles.

l: Elatea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Elatea is next to Delphi the greatest town in Phocis, opposite Amphiclea and 180 stades away by road. Its people repulsed Cassander and the Macedonians, resisted Taxilus and the barbarians from Pontus, and received freedom and immunity from taxation from the Romans. Elatea contains a handsome market-place, a figure of Elatus, a temple of Æsculapius, a theatre, and an ancient bronze statue of Athene.

l: Phocis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Phocis contains Elatea, which is described as one of its towns. Elatea shared in the general disasters of the Phocians and was one of the towns in Phocis burned by the Mede.

l: Cassander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Cassander blockaded Elatea with an army, but Olympiodorus mainly rendered the blockade inoperative.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Macedonians, under Cassander, were repulsed by the Elateans. Under Philip, the son of Demetrius, they retained Elatea until the town was reduced by the blockade of the Romans.

l: Taxilus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Taxilus, the general of Mithridates, attacked Elatea, but the Elateans held out against him. Their resistance to Taxilus and the barbarians from Pontus led the Romans to grant them freedom and immunity from taxation.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Romans granted the Elateans freedom and immunity from taxation after their resistance to Taxilus and the barbarians from Pontus. Titus Flaminius was sent from Rome to free all Greece and invited Elatea to revolt from the Macedonians.

l: Elatus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Elatus, said to be the son of Areas, defended the god when the men of Phlegyas attacked the temple at Delphi and then founded Elatea. A figure of Elatus stands on a pillar in the market-place at Elatea, either in his honour as founder or to mark his tomb.

l: Olympiodorus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Olympiodorus mainly rendered Cassander's blockade of Elatea inoperative.

l: Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Philip, the son of Demetrius, inspired great terror among the people of Elatea and won over the most influential townsfolk by bribes. Under him, Elatea remained faithful to the Macedonians instead of accepting Titus Flaminius's invitation to revolt.

l: Flaminius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Titus Flaminius, the Roman General sent from Rome to free all Greece, promised Elatea its ancient polity and invited it to revolt from the Macedonians.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Titus Flaminius was sent from Rome to free all Greece. In the speaker's day, the Costoboci overran all Greece before coming to Elatea.

l: blockade of Elatea by the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The blockade of Elatea by the Romans reduced the town after it remained faithful to Philip, the son of Demetrius, rather than revolting from the Macedonians.

l: barbarians from Pontus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The barbarians from Pontus joined Taxilus in attacking Elatea. The Elateans held out against them, and their resistance helped earn the town freedom and immunity from taxation from the Romans.

l: freedom, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Freedom and immunity from taxation were granted to the Elateans by the Romans for their successful resistance to Taxilus and the barbarians from Pontus.

l: Costoboci, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Costoboci were a piratical tribe that overran all Greece in the speaker's day and came to Elatea. Mnesibulus assembled picked men against them, slew many of them, and fell in the battle.

l: Mnesibulus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Mnesibulus gathered an army of picked men when the Costoboci came to Elatea, slew many of the barbarians, and died in the battle. He had won several victories and, in the 235th Olympiad, won both the stadium and the double course while carrying his shield; a brazen statue of him stood near the race-course.

l: Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: An ancient bronze statue of Athene stood in the theatre at the extreme right of Elatea. The Elateans said that Athene fought for them against the barbarians under Taxilus.

l: Athene Cranæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Athene Cranæa has a temple about 20 stades from Elatea. Her statue was armed for battle and imitated the shield of Athene in the Parthenon at Athens.

l: temple of Athene Cranæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The temple of Athene Cranæa stands on the mostly precipitous crest of a hill reached by an easy uphill road from Elatea. It has porticoes and chambers for those who minister to the goddess, especially the priest, who is chosen from the youths, serves for five continuous years, resides with the goddess, and bathes in tubs according to the ancient manner.

l: statue of Athene Cranæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The statue of Athene Cranæa was made by the sons of Polycles. It is armed for battle, and its shield imitates the shield of Athene in the Parthenon at Athens.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The unit describes Abæ and Hyampolis in Phocis, including their origins, ruins, sanctuaries, water supplies, and civic buildings. Abæ was associated with Apollo and had a temple destroyed first by Xerxes’ army and later by the Thebans during the Phocian War. Hyampolis was founded by Hyantes who fled Thebes and especially worshipped Artemis. The text also describes the road from Chæronea to Phocis and the town of Stiris, whose inhabitants claimed Athenian origins and worshipped Demeter Stiritis.

l: Abæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Abæ was said by its people to have been founded by Abas, son of Lynceus and Hypermnestra, and its inhabitants claimed to have come to Phocis from Argos. They considered the town sacred to Apollo and possessed an ancient theatre and market-place.

l: Hyampolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Hyampolis was said to have been founded by Hyantes who fled Thebes and was originally called the town of the Hyantes. Although Xerxes burnt it and Philip razed it, the town retained remains of its market-place, council-chamber, and theatre, as well as a Portico built by the Emperor Adrian; its inhabitants relied mainly on one well and winter rainwater.

l: Stiris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Stiris was said by its inhabitants to have been founded by Athenians who came with Peteus, son of Orneus, after his expulsion from Athens by Ægeus. It stood on high, rocky ground with poor water supplies, and contained a temple of Demeter Stiritis and another ancient statue dedicated to Demeter.

l: Phocis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Phocis could be reached from Chæronea either by the road through Panopeus and Daulis or by the rugged mountain road to Stiris. Abæ and Stiris are described in connection with the region, and the Phocian War affected the temple at Abæ.

l: Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Chæronea was the starting point for routes into Phocis, including a direct road to Delphi through Panopeus and Daulis and a mountainous road to Stiris measuring 120 stades.

l: Xerxes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Xerxes’ army burnt the temple at Abæ and also burnt Hyampolis.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Apollo was especially associated with Abæ, where the inhabitants considered the town sacred to him and maintained an oracle. The Romans granted the people of Abæ autonomy in their piety to Apollo, and the Emperor Adrian later erected a smaller temple to him there.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Artemis was the goddess especially worshipped at Hyampolis, which had a temple dedicated to her. The temple was opened only twice a year, and cattle considered sacred to Artemis were said to be healthier and fatter than other cattle.

l: Temple of Apollo at Abæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The ancient temple of Apollo at Abæ was burnt by Xerxes’ army and later set on fire by the Thebans during the Phocian War while Phocian fugitives had taken refuge there. It was therefore described as the most ruinous of the fire-damaged buildings; a smaller temple built by the Emperor Adrian stood nearby, containing ancient bronze statues of Apollo, Leto, and Artemis dedicated by the people of Abæ.

l: Temple of Demeter Stiritis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The Temple of Demeter Stiritis at Stiris was built of unbaked brick. Its statue of Demeter was made of Pentelican marble and showed her holding torches.

l: Phocian War, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: During the Phocian War, Thebans set fire to the Temple of Apollo at Abæ while Phocian fugitives who had been defeated in battle were seeking refuge there.

l: Persian destruction of Abæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The Persian destruction of Abæ included the burning of its Temple of Apollo by Xerxes’ army. The temple was later consumed altogether by a Theban fire during the Phocian War.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: The road from Stiris to Ambrosus crosses a vine-growing plain where coccus grows and is collected for wool dyeing. Ambrosus lies beneath Mount Parnassus opposite Delphi and has double defensive walls built during the war against Philip and the Macedonians. The road onward leads to Anticyra, whose ancient name was Cyparissus and whose inhabitants were expelled twice for their political loyalties. Anticyra contains sanctuaries, gymnasiums, a conduit, and a tomb associated with the sons of Iphitus.

l: Stiris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Stiris is the starting point of the road to Ambrosus, which is about 60 stades away.

l: Ambrosus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Ambrosus lies beneath Mount Parnassus and opposite Delphi, and is said to have been named after the hero Ambrosus. During the war against Philip and the Macedonians, the Thebans built double walls around it. It has a small market-place with mostly broken stone statues, and the road from it leads downhill toward Anticyra.

l: coccus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Coccus grows in the plain between Stiris and Ambrosus, though less plentifully than vines. Its berry is gathered while it contains a grub, because the grub's blood is useful for dyeing wool; the Ionians and Greeks call it coccus, while the Galati above Phrygia call it Hys.

l: Parnassus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Mount Parnassus lies above Ambrosus.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Delphi lies opposite Ambrosus. Medeon is identified as one of the towns that impiously plundered the temple at Delphi.

l: double walls of Ambrosus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: The Thebans built the double walls during the war against Philip and the Macedonians. They were made of the district's black, very strong stone; each wall had a circumference of little less than a fathom and stood 2½ fathoms high where intact, with a fathom between the walls. Built for immediate defence, they had no towers, battlements, or other embellishment.

l: Anticyra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Anticyra was formerly called Cyparissus and was said to have received its later name from Anticyreus, a contemporary of Hercules. It lies below the ruins of Medeon, and its people were expelled first by Philip son of Amyntas and later by the Roman Otilius for supporting Philip son of Demetrius, king of the Macedonians. Anticyra has brazen statues in its market-place, a small temple of Poseidon near the harbour, two gymnasiums, a conduit, and a tomb said to belong to the sons of Iphitus.

l: temple of Dictynnæan Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: A temple of Dictynnæan Artemis stands about two stades from Ambrosus on the road to Anticyra. Its statue of the goddess is made in the Aeginetan style from black stone.

l: Dictynnæan Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Dictynnæan Artemis is held in the highest honour by the people of Ambrosus. Her statue in the temple near Ambrosus is of black stone and Aeginetan workmanship.

l: Medeon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Medeon lies in ruins above Anticyra. It was one of the towns that impiously plundered the temple at Delphi.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The unit describes Bulis, its location and temples, and the route between it, Anticyra, and nearby ports. It then discusses the road from Delphi to Cirrha, including Apollo’s Hippodrome and the treeless plain. Cirrha is said to have violated Apollo’s sacred territory, leading the Amphictyones, under Clisthenes with Solon’s advice, to wage war against it. Solon diverted the river Plistus and poisoned its water with hellebore, enabling the Amphictyones to capture Cirrha and make it the seaport of Delphi.

l: Anticyra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Anticyra is about 100 stades from the port near Bulis. The text is uncertain whether a mainland road connects Anticyra with Bulis because of the precipitous mountains between them.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Artemis has a temple on a lofty rock about two stades from the town, with a statue by Praxiteles holding a torch and accompanied by a dog. Bulis also has a temple of Artemis with a wooden statue.

l: Bulis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Bulis is a town bordering Phocis, founded by Bulon and colonized from the towns of ancient Doris. Its inhabitants were said to have shared in the impiety of Philomelus and the Phocians, and more than half lived by catching shellfish for purple dye. Bulis had temples of Artemis and Dionysus, worshipped a god called Supreme, and possessed a well called Saunion.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Cirrha is the seaport of Delphi and lies about 60 stades from Delphi. The road descending from Delphi to the plain passes an Hippodrome where the Pythian horse-races are held.

l: Cirrha, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Cirrha was also called Crisa by Homer and was said to have taken its present name from the Nymph Cirrha. Its people committed acts of impiety against Apollo and ravaged land sacred to him, after which the Amphictyones captured the town and punished its inhabitants. Cirrha then became the seaport of Delphi and contained a temple of Apollo, Artemis, and Leto, with Attic statues, as well as a smaller statue of Adrastea.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Apollo has a Hippodrome near Delphi where the Pythian horse-races are held, and accidents sometimes occur there. Cirrha’s people were said to have committed impiety against Apollo and ravaged his sacred territory, and Cirrha later contained a temple of Apollo, Artemis, and Leto.

l: Amphictyones, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The Amphictyones resolved to wage war against the people of Cirrha because of their impiety toward Apollo. They chose Clisthenes as leader, sought Solon’s counsel, consecrated the land around Cirrha to Apollo, captured the town, and took vengeance on its inhabitants.

l: Solon of Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Solon advised the Amphictyones to consecrate the land around Cirrha to Apollo so that the god’s grove would extend to the sea. He also devised the plan of diverting the river Plistus and using hellebore to make its water disable the besieged people of Cirrha.

l: river Plistus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The river Plistus flowed through Cirrha until Solon had it diverted. Solon threw hellebore roots into the diverted river and then restored its course, causing those who drank the water to suffer incessant diarrhoea.

l: war against Cirrha, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The Amphictyones waged war against Cirrha after its people committed impious acts against Apollo and ravaged his sacred territory. Clisthenes led the war, while Solon assisted with his counsel.

l: siege of Cirrha, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: During the siege, the people of Cirrha continued to hold out by drinking rainwater and water from wells. After Solon’s manipulation of the river Plistus caused them to suffer incessant diarrhoea, they could no longer man the walls, and the Amphictyones captured the town.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The unit describes the Ozolian Locrians, the traditions explaining their name, and their principal towns. Amphissa is presented as their largest and most famous town, with tombs, temples, and an imported statue of Athene. Myonia and Œanthea are also described, while Naupactus receives an account of its name, history, sanctuaries, and the healing of Phalysius. Except for Amphissa, these towns were under the Achæans of Patræ by a grant from the Emperor Augustus.

l: Locrians called Ozolæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Ozolian Locrians occupied the region around Amphissa, Myonia, Œanthea, and Naupactus. The text gives several traditions for their name, and says that the inhabitants of Amphissa joined themselves to the Ætolians because they were ashamed of the title Ozolian.

l: Amphissa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Amphissa was about 120 stades from Delphi and was the largest and most famous town of the Ozolian Locrians. It contained the tombs of Amphissa and Andræmon, a temple and statue of Athene in its citadel, and celebrated rites for youths called Anactes. The inhabitants later joined themselves to the Ætolians, and many Ætolians may also have migrated there after Augustus established Nicopolis.

l: Myonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Myonia lay above Amphissa, about 30 stades away, facing the mainland. Its inhabitants presented a shield to Zeus at Olympia, and the town had a grove and altar of the Mild Deities where nightly sacrifices were performed, as well as a grove and temple of Poseidon called Poseidonium.

l: Œanthea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Œanthea lay near the sea and was one of the towns, other than Amphissa, placed under the Achæans of Patræ by a grant from the Emperor Augustus. It had a temple of Aphrodite, and a nearby grove of cypress and pine containing a temple and statue of Artemis, along with wall paintings obscured by time. The text suggests that its name may have come from a woman or a Nymph.

l: Naupactus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Naupactus lay near Œanthea and was said to have been named because the Dorians and the sons of Aristomachus built a fleet there to cross to the Peloponnese. The town passed from the Locrians to the Athenians, then to the Messenians, and finally back to the Locrians after the Lacedæmonians expelled the Messenians. It contained temples and statues of Poseidon, Artemis, and Aphrodite, ruins of a temple of Æsculapius, and was the place where Phalysius was cured of blindness after receiving a sealed letter from the god of Epidaurus through Anyte.

l: origin of the name Ozolian, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: One tradition says that Orestheus, son of Deucalion, buried a piece of wood born from a bitch, from which a vine grew the next spring; the Locrians supposedly took their name from its branches. Other traditions connect the name with the rotting body of Nessus, the unpleasant smell of a river, the smell of abundant asphodel, or the odor of untanned hides worn by the first inhabitants.

l: The Library, The Library, The Library
s: Uranus was the first ruler of the entire universe. After marrying Earth, he fathered the Hecatoncheires: Briareus, Gyges, and Cottus. They were extraordinarily large and powerful, with one hundred hands and fifty heads each. The text also discusses the marriage of Sky and Earth as a widespread myth.

l: Apollodorus, The Library, The Library
s: Apollodorus is identified with The Library in the heading of the unit.

l: The Library, The Library, The Library
s: The Library presents Uranus as the first ruler of the entire universe and recounts his marriage to Earth and the birth of the Hecatoncheires.

l: Sky, The Library, The Library
s: Uranus was the first to rule the entire universe. He married Earth and fathered Briareus, Gyges, and Cottus, who were called the Hecatoncheires.

l: Earth, The Library, The Library
s: Earth married Uranus and bore the Hecatoncheires: Briareus, Gyges, and Cottus.

l: the Hecatoncheires, The Library, The Library
s: The Hecatoncheires were Briareus, Gyges, and Cottus. Each was exceptionally large and powerful, possessing one hundred hands and fifty heads.

l: Briareus, The Library, The Library
s: Briareus was one of the Hecatoncheires born to Uranus and Earth. He was extraordinarily large and powerful and had one hundred hands and fifty heads.

l: Gyges, The Library, The Library
s: Gyges was one of the Hecatoncheires born to Uranus and Earth. He was extraordinarily large and powerful and had one hundred hands and fifty heads.

l: Cottus, The Library, The Library
s: Cottus was one of the Hecatoncheires born to Uranus and Earth. He was extraordinarily large and powerful and had one hundred hands and fifty heads.

l: the marriage of Sky and Earth, The Library, The Library
s: The marriage of Sky and Earth is presented as a myth in which Sky and Earth are joined. The text notes that this myth is widespread among lower races.

l: The Library, The Library, BOOK I
s: Sky first ruled the whole world and fathered the Hundred-handed, the Cyclopes, and the Titans with Earth. Sky cast the Cyclopes into Tartarus, while Earth persuaded the Titans to attack him, and Cronus overthrew him with an adamantine sickle. Cronus then ruled, but he swallowed his children because of a prophecy that he would be dethroned by his own son. Rhea secretly gave birth to Zeus in a cave of Dicte and arranged for him to be raised in Crete while Cronus swallowed a stone in his place.

l: Sky, The Library, BOOK I
s: Sky was the first ruler of the whole world. With Earth, he fathered the Hundred-handed, the Cyclopes, and the Titans; he bound the Cyclopes and cast them into Tartarus. The Titans later attacked him, and Cronus cut off his genitals and overthrew him.

l: Earth, The Library, BOOK I
s: Earth was the mate of Sky and the mother of the Hundred-handed, the Cyclopes, and the Titans. Grieved because Sky had cast some of her children into Tartarus, she persuaded the Titans to attack him and gave Cronus an adamantine sickle.

l: Tartarus, The Library, BOOK I
s: Tartarus is a gloomy place in Hades, as far from Earth as Earth is from Sky. Sky cast the Cyclopes into it, and Cronus later bound and shut them there again.

l: Titans, The Library, BOOK I
s: The Titans were children of Sky and Earth. Except for Ocean, they attacked Sky after Earth persuaded them, and they brought their brothers who had been cast into Tartarus back out before giving the rule to Cronus.

l: Cronus, The Library, BOOK I
s: Cronus was the youngest of the Titans and used an adamantine sickle to cut off Sky's genitals and overthrow him. He became ruler, but again imprisoned the Cyclopes in Tartarus and swallowed his children because of the prophecy that his own son would dethrone him. When Rhea gave him a stone wrapped as a newborn child, he swallowed the stone instead of Zeus.

l: Rhea, The Library, BOOK I
s: Rhea became the wife of Cronus and was the mother of Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Pluto, Poseidon, and Zeus. Angry because Cronus swallowed her children, she went to Crete while pregnant with Zeus, gave birth to him in a cave of Dicte, and gave Cronus a wrapped stone to swallow in his place.

l: prophecy of Cronus's dethronement, The Library, BOOK I
s: The prophecy stated that Cronus would be deprived of his rule by his own child. Earth and Sky foretold it, causing Cronus to swallow each child born to him until Rhea concealed Zeus.

l: Dicte, The Library, BOOK I
s: Dicte was the place in Crete where Rhea gave birth to Zeus in a cave. She entrusted Zeus to the Curetes and the nymphs Adrastia and Ida to be raised there.

l: Zeus, The Library, BOOK I
s: Zeus was the son of Cronus and Rhea. Rhea gave birth to him secretly in a cave of Dicte and arranged for the Curetes and the nymphs Adrastia and Ida to nurse and guard him, while Cronus swallowed a stone believing it was the newborn child.

l: The Library, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: When Zeus becomes full-grown, he takes Metis, daughter of Ocean, as his helper, and she gives Cronus a drug that makes him disgorge the stone and the children he had swallowed. With these children Zeus wages a ten-year war against Cronus and the Titans, following Earth’s prophecy that victory will come if he allies with those imprisoned in Tartarus. Zeus frees the Cyclopes, who provide divine weapons, and the gods defeat and imprison the Titans in Tartarus under the guard of the Hundred-handers. Zeus, Poseidon, and Pluto then divide sovereignty among the sky, sea, and Hades.

l: Zeus, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: When Zeus becomes full-grown, he takes Metis as his helper and wages war against Cronus and the Titans with the aid of the children Cronus had swallowed. He frees the Cyclopes, receives thunder, lightning, and a thunderbolt from them, defeats the Titans, and is allotted sovereignty over the sky.

l: Metis, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: Metis, the daughter of Ocean, helps Zeus by giving Cronus a drug to swallow. The drug forces Cronus to disgorge the stone and the children he had swallowed.

l: Cronus, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: Cronus swallows a drug given by Metis and is forced to disgorge first the stone and then the children he had swallowed. Zeus and those children subsequently wage war against him and the Titans.

l: children swallowed by Cronus, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: The children swallowed by Cronus are disgorged after he takes the drug given by Metis. They assist Zeus in his war against Cronus and the Titans.

l: war against Cronus and the Titans, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: The war lasts ten years. Earth prophesies victory to Zeus if he has as allies those who were hurled down to Tartarus, and Zeus and his allies ultimately defeat the Titans.

l: Titans, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: The Titans fight Zeus and his allies for ten years. They are defeated, shut up in Tartarus, and placed under the guard of the Hundred-handers.

l: Tartarus, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: Tartarus is the place to which certain allies of Zeus had been hurled and from which Zeus releases them. The defeated Titans are imprisoned there, with the Hundred-handers appointed as their guards.

l: Cyclopes, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: Zeus frees the Cyclopes from their bonds after killing Campe, who guarded them. The Cyclopes give Zeus thunder, lightning, and a thunderbolt; they give Pluto a helmet and Poseidon a trident.

l: Pluto, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: Pluto receives a helmet from the Cyclopes. When the gods divide sovereignty by lot, he is allotted dominion in Hades.

l: Poseidon, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: Poseidon receives a trident from the Cyclopes. When the gods divide sovereignty by lot, he is allotted dominion over the sea.

l: sovereignty, The Library, II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει
s: The gods cast lots for sovereignty after defeating the Titans. Zeus receives dominion over the sky, Poseidon dominion over the sea, and Pluto dominion in Hades.

l: The Library, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: The unit concerns Zeus’s offspring and unions, including his children by Hera, Themis, Dione, Eurynome, Styx, and Mnemosyne. It recounts the stories of Orpheus and Eurydice, Hyacinth and Apollo, Thamyris and the Muses, and several children born from the Muses. It also describes Hera’s birth of Hephaestus and Zeus’s swallowing of Metis, after which Athena emerged from his head fully armed.

l: Zeus, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Zeus married Hera and fathered Hebe, Ilithyia, and Ares with her. He fathered Aphrodite by Dione, the Graces by Eurynome, Persephone by Styx, and the Muses by Mnemosyne, and he had intercourse with many mortal and immortal women. He swallowed Metis while she was pregnant, and Athena later emerged from his head.

l: Hera, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Hera married Zeus and bore Hebe, Ilithyia, and Ares. She gave birth to Hephaestus without intercourse, though Homer says that Zeus was also his father. Zeus hung Hera from Olympus after she sent a storm against Heracles.

l: Aphrodite, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Aphrodite was born to Zeus and Dione. Clio incurred her wrath by reproaching her for her love of Adonis.

l: Muses, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: The Muses were daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne. They defeated Thamyris in a musical contest and deprived him of his eyes and his minstrelsy.

l: Calliope, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Calliope was the first of the Muses listed. She bore Linus and Orpheus to Oeagrus, or nominally to Apollo, and some said that Rhesus was her son.

l: Apollo, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Apollo was named as the nominal father of Linus and Orpheus. He loved Hyacinth and accidentally killed him with a discus.

l: Orpheus, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Orpheus was the son of Calliope and Oeagrus, or nominally of Apollo. He practised minstrelsy, moved stones and trees by singing, and went to Hades to bring back his wife Eurydice; after turning to look at her, he lost her again. He also instituted the mysteries of Dionysus and was torn to pieces by the Maenads before being buried in Pieria.

l: Eurydice, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Eurydice was Orpheus’s wife. She died after being bitten by a snake, and when Orpheus turned to look at her while bringing her from Hades, she returned there.

l: Hyacinth, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Hyacinth was the son of Clio and Pierus. Apollo loved him and accidentally killed him by throwing a discus.

l: Thamyris, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Thamyris was the son of Philammon and the nymph Argiope. He fell in love with Hyacinth and was the first to become enamoured of males. He challenged the Muses to a musical contest, was defeated, and lost both his eyes and his minstrelsy.

l: Hephaestus, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Hephaestus was born to Hera without intercourse, though Homer says that Zeus was also his father. Zeus cast him from heaven when he came to Hera’s aid, and he fell on Lemnos and was lamed in his legs before Thetis saved him.

l: Metis, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Metis had intercourse with Zeus and changed into many forms to avoid him. After she became pregnant, Zeus swallowed her because he feared that her future child would become ruler of heaven.

l: Athena, The Library, III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ
s: Athena emerged fully armed from the top of Zeus’s head after his head was struck with an axe.

l: The Library, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Asteria fled Zeus by taking the form of a quail and throwing herself into the sea, after which the island was first called Asteria and later Delos. Hera pursued Leto across the earth until Leto reached Delos, where Artemis was born first and later helped deliver Apollo. Apollo took over the oracle at Delphi after killing Python, and he also killed Tityus and Marsyas. Artemis killed Orion, whose stories include his blinding by Oenopion, his restoration of sight, and different accounts of his death.

l: Asteria, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Asteria took the form of a quail and threw herself into the sea to escape Zeus's amorous advances. The island formerly called Asteria was later called Delos.

l: Zeus, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Zeus pursued Asteria and Leto. He was the father of Apollo, Artemis, and Tityus according to the accounts given in this unit.

l: Delos, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Delos was formerly called Asteria. Leto reached Delos while fleeing Hera and gave birth there first to Artemis and later to Apollo; Artemis also killed Orion there, and Dawn brought Orion there.

l: Leto, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Leto was pursued by Hera throughout the earth because of her union with Zeus. When she reached Delos, she gave birth first to Artemis and later, assisted by Artemis, to Apollo.

l: Hera, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Hera drove Leto across the whole earth. She also cast Side into Hades because Side rivalled her in beauty.

l: Artemis, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Artemis was born on Delos before Apollo and helped Leto give birth to him. She devoted herself to hunting and remained a virgin, killed Tityus and Orion, and was said either to have killed Orion for challenging her to a contest at quoits or to have shot him for offering violence to Opis.

l: Apollo, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Apollo learned prophecy from Pan and came to Delphi, where he killed Python and took over the oracle. He killed Tityus, defeated and killed Marsyas in a musical contest, and was born on Delos after Artemis.

l: Delphi, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: At Delphi, Themis was delivering oracles when Apollo arrived. Python guarded the oracle there and prevented Apollo from approaching the chasm until Apollo killed it.

l: Python, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Python was a snake guarding the oracle at Delphi. It prevented Apollo from approaching the chasm, but Apollo killed it and took over the oracle.

l: oracle of Delphi, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: The oracle of Delphi was being delivered by Themis when Apollo arrived. After killing Python, Apollo took over the oracle.

l: Tityus, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Tityus was described as a son of Zeus and Elare and as a monstrous-sized child brought from beneath the earth. He attempted to seize Leto, was shot by her children, and was punished after death when vultures ate his heart in Hades.

l: Marsyas, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Marsyas was the son of Olympus and found the pipes that Athena had thrown away. He competed musically with Apollo, lost because he could not turn his pipes upside down, and was hanged from a pine and flayed by Apollo.

l: Athena, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Athena threw away the pipes because playing them disfigured her face. Marsyas found the discarded pipes and used them in his musical contest with Apollo.

l: musical contest between Apollo and Marsyas, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Apollo and Marsyas agreed that the victor could do whatever he wished to the defeated contestant. Apollo turned his lyre upside down and ordered Marsyas to do the same with his pipes; when Marsyas could not, Apollo was judged the victor and killed him.

l: Orion, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Orion was described as gigantic and earth-born, though Pherecydes said he was the son of Poseidon and Euryale. Poseidon gave him the power to stride across the sea; Oenopion blinded him, but he regained his sight through the sun's rays. Orion was killed by Artemis according to differing accounts, either for challenging her to a contest at quoits or for offering violence to Opis.

l: Poseidon, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: According to Pherecydes, Poseidon was Orion's father. He gave Orion the power to stride across the sea and made an underground house constructed by Hephaestus for Oenopion.

l: Oenopion, The Library, IV. Τῶν δὲ Κοίου θυγατέρων ᾿Αστερία μὲν
s: Oenopion's daughter Merope was wooed by Orion. Oenopion made Orion drunk, blinded him while he slept, and threw him onto the beach; Poseidon later prepared an underground house for Oenopion.

l: The Library, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Pluto, with Zeus’s help, secretly abducts Persephone. Demeter searches for Persephone throughout the earth and, after learning that Pluto took her, comes to Eleusis in the guise of a woman. Persephone eats a pomegranate seed given by Pluto and is required to spend one-third of each year with him and the rest with the gods.

l: Pluto, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Pluto falls in love with Persephone and, with Zeus’s help, secretly carries her off. He gives Persephone a pomegranate seed to eat so that she will not remain with Demeter for long.

l: Zeus, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Zeus helps Pluto secretly carry off Persephone. Later, Zeus orders Pluto to send Persephone back.

l: Persephone, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Persephone is secretly carried off by Pluto. She eats a pomegranate seed in the underworld and is therefore required to spend one-third of each year with Pluto and the rest with the gods.

l: Demeter, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Demeter searches throughout the earth for Persephone with torches by night and day. After learning that Pluto abducted Persephone, she leaves heaven in anger and comes to Eleusis disguised as a woman.

l: earth, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Demeter searches all over the earth for Persephone.

l: Eleusis, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Demeter comes to Eleusis in the likeness of a woman. She first sits on the Laughless Rock beside the Well of the Fair Dances and then goes to the house of Celeus.

l: pomegranate seed, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Pluto gives Persephone a pomegranate seed to eat. Persephone eats it without foreseeing the consequence.

l: the underworld division of Persephone’s time, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Persephone is compelled to remain one-third of every year with Pluto and to spend the remaining time with the gods.

l: the abduction of Persephone, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Pluto secretly abducts Persephone with the help of Zeus. Demeter learns from the people of Hermion that Pluto carried her off.

l: Demeter’s search for Persephone, The Library, V. Πλούτων δὲ Περσεφόνης ἐρασθεὶς Διὸς
s: Demeter searches for Persephone throughout the earth with torches by night and day. Her search leads her to Hermion and then to Eleusis.

l: The Library, The Library, VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"
s: Earth, angered over the Titans, gives birth to the Giants, who attack the sky and are defeated by the gods with the aid of Heracles. Zeus learns that the Giants can be killed only with the help of a mortal, obtains a herb that would protect them, and summons Heracles through Athena. After the Giants are overcome, Earth unites with Tartarus and gives birth to Typhon, whom Zeus eventually defeats by casting Mount Etna upon him.

l: Earth, The Library, VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"
s: Earth, angered over the Titans, gives birth to the Giants by Sky. She seeks a herb to prevent the Giants from being destroyed even by a mortal, but Zeus obtains it first. After the Giants are defeated, Earth, still more enraged, unites with Tartarus and gives birth to Typhon in Cilicia.

l: Giants, The Library, VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"
s: The Giants are born from Earth and Sky, possessing enormous bodies, great strength, terrifying appearances, dragon scales for feet, and the ability to hurl rocks and burning oaks at the sky. Porphyrion and Alcyoneus surpass the others; Alcyoneus is immortal while fighting in his native land and has driven away the Sun’s cows from Erythia. The Giants are defeated by the gods with the help of Heracles, who shoots the dying Giants with arrows, while Zeus destroys many of them with thunderbolts.

l: Zeus, The Library, VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"
s: Zeus learns that the Giants cannot be killed by gods alone but can be destroyed with the help of a mortal. He prevents the Dawn, Moon, and Sun from shining, obtains the herb sought by Earth, and summons Heracles through Athena. During the battle he strikes Porphyrion with a thunderbolt, destroys other Giants with thunderbolts, and later defeats Typhon after recovering his severed sinews.

l: Hercules, The Library, VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"
s: Heracles is summoned by Athena to aid the gods against the Giants. He shoots Alcyoneus, drags him outside Pallene so that he can die, kills Porphyrion after Zeus strikes him with a thunderbolt, and helps destroy the other Giants by shooting them with arrows. He later joins Zeus in the battle against Typhon by helping restore Zeus’s sinews.

l: Athena, The Library, VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"
s: Athena summons Heracles to aid the gods against the Giants and advises him to drag Alcyoneus outside Pallene. She throws the island of Sicily upon the fleeing Enceladus and flays Pallas, using his skin to cover and protect her body in the battle.

l: Typhon, The Library, VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"
s: Typhon is born in Cilicia from Earth and Tartarus after the defeat of the Giants. He is a vast hybrid of man and beast, with dragon heads, serpent coils, wings, fire-filled eyes, and great destructive power. Zeus wounds and pursues him, but Typhon severs Zeus’s hand and foot sinews and hides them in the Corycian cave; Hermes and Aegipan recover and restore them, after which Zeus pursues Typhon through several regions and finally buries him under Mount Etna.

l: war of the gods and Giants, The Library, VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"
s: The war begins when the Giants attack the sky by hurling rocks and burning oaks. The gods receive an oracle that the Giants can be destroyed only with the aid of a mortal, so Zeus summons Heracles through Athena. The gods and Heracles defeat the Giants, with each combatant being killed or overcome by various gods, Heracles, or Zeus.

l: The Library, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Prometheus moulds human beings from water and earth and secretly gives them fire carried in a fennel stalk. Zeus punishes Prometheus by having him nailed to Mount Caucasus, where an eagle eats his liver daily, until Hercules later releases him. Prometheus's son Deucalion survives Zeus's Flood with Pyrrha in a chest, lands on Mount Parnassus, and restores humankind by throwing stones that become men and women.

l: Typhon, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Typhon is pursued by Zeus after Zeus recovers his strength. He flees through Thrace and the Sicilian sea, and Zeus buries him under Mount Etna.

l: Zeus, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Zeus pursues Typhon with thunderbolts and buries him under Mount Etna. He punishes Prometheus for giving fire to human beings by ordering Hephaestus to nail him to Mount Caucasus. Zeus later sends Hermes to Deucalion and allows him to choose what he wants.

l: Prometheus, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Prometheus moulds human beings from water and earth and secretly gives them fire hidden in a fennel stalk. Zeus has him nailed to Mount Caucasus, where an eagle eats his liver each day as it grows back during the night. Hercules later releases him.

l: human beings, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Prometheus moulds human beings from water and earth. Zeus's Flood destroys nearly all human beings, but the stones thrown by Deucalion and Pyrrha become men and women.

l: fire, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Prometheus gives fire to human beings after secretly hiding it in a fennel stalk. Zeus punishes Prometheus for this theft.

l: Hercules, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Hercules later releases Prometheus from his bonds on Mount Caucasus.

l: Deucalion, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Deucalion, the son of Prometheus, rules the regions around Phthia and marries Pyrrha. On Prometheus's advice, he constructs a chest, enters it with Pyrrha, survives the Flood, lands on Mount Parnassus, and throws stones that become men.

l: Pyrrha, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Pyrrha, the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, marries Deucalion. She survives the Flood with him in the chest and throws stones that become women.

l: Deucalion's chest, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Deucalion constructs the chest on Prometheus's advice and stores provisions in it. He and Pyrrha enter it and float over the sea for nine days and nights during the Flood.

l: Greece, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Zeus floods most of Greece with heavy rain, destroying its inhabitants except for those who escape to nearby high mountains.

l: Mount Parnassus, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Deucalion and Pyrrha drift to Mount Parnassus in the chest. They land there after the rains stop.

l: stones, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: Deucalion and Pyrrha throw stones over their heads at the bidding of Zeus. Deucalion's stones become men, and Pyrrha's stones become women.

l: Deucalion’s flood, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: The Flood occurs when Zeus pours heavy rain from heaven. It destroys most of Greece and its human beings, while Deucalion and Pyrrha survive in their chest.

l: the theft of fire, The Library, VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-
s: The theft of fire is committed by Prometheus when he secretly takes fire and gives it to human beings. Zeus punishes him for the theft by having him bound on Mount Caucasus.

l: The Library, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Hellen, said by some to be the son of Zeus, had Dorus, Xuthus, and Aeolus by Orseis and divided the country among them. He named the Greeks Hellenes after himself, while his sons gave their names to the Dorians, Achaeans, Ionians, and Aeolians. Poseidon fathered Otus and Ephialtes, the Aloads, who tried to attack the gods but were killed by Artemis through deception. Endymion became ruler of Elis, and his son Aetolus later gave his name to Aetolia.

l: Hellen, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Some say that Hellen was born from Zeus. By the nymph Orseis he had Dorus, Xuthus, and Aeolus, named the Greeks Hellenes after himself, and divided the country among his sons.

l: Zeus, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Some say that Zeus was the father of Hellen. Zeus also fathered Aethlius by Protogonia and turned Ceyx and Alcyone into birds after their claim that she was Hera and he was Zeus.

l: Dorus, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Dorus was a son of Hellen and Orseis. He received the country beyond Peloponnese and called its inhabitants Dorians after himself.

l: Xuthus, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Xuthus was a son of Hellen and Orseis. He received Peloponnese and fathered Achaeus and Ion by Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus.

l: Aeolus, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Aeolus was a son of Hellen and Orseis. He ruled the regions around Thessaly and named their inhabitants Aeolians; by Enarete he had seven sons and five daughters.

l: Greeks, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: The people called Greeks were renamed Hellenes by Hellen.

l: Hellenes, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: The Hellenes were the people whom Hellen named after himself from among those previously called Greeks.

l: Peloponnese, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Peloponnese was received by Xuthus, who fathered Achaeus and Ion there by Creusa.

l: Poseidon, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Poseidon fathered Hopleus, Nireus, Epopeus, Aloeus, and Triops by Canace. By Iphimedia he fathered Otus and Ephialtes, who were called the Aloads.

l: Otus, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Otus was fathered by Poseidon and Iphimedia and was called one of the Aloads. He wooed Artemis, helped threaten the gods, and was killed in Naxos when Artemis, disguised as a deer, caused him and Ephialtes to spear each other.

l: Ephialtes, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Ephialtes was fathered by Poseidon and Iphimedia and was called one of the Aloads. He wooed Hera, helped threaten the gods, and was killed in Naxos when Artemis, disguised as a deer, caused him and Otus to spear each other.

l: Aloads, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: The Aloads were Otus and Ephialtes, sons of Poseidon and Iphimedia. They grew rapidly, attempted to pile mountains to reach heaven, threatened to reshape the sea and land, imprisoned Ares, and were killed by Artemis through deception.

l: Endymion, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Endymion was the son of Calyce and Aethlius, though some said he was born from Zeus. He led Aeolians from Thessaly, settled Elis, and was loved by Selene; Zeus granted him the choice of what he wished, and he chose eternal sleep while remaining immortal and ageless.

l: Aetolus, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Aetolus was the son of Endymion and either a Naiad nymph or Iphianassa. After killing Apis, son of Phoroneus, he fled to the land of the Curetes, killed Phthias and Apollo's sons Dorus, Laodocus, and Polypoetes, and named the country Aetolia after himself.

l: Aetolia, The Library, Ἕλλην μὲν πρῶτος, ὃν ἐκ Atos γεγεννῆσθαι ϊ
s: Aetolia was named after Aetolus, who had fled there and killed those who received him, including Phthias and Apollo's sons Dorus, Laodocus, and Polypoetes.

l: The Library, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: The unit traces the descendants of Porthaon and Thestius and describes the family of Oeneus, king of Calydon. Oeneus neglected Artemis in a sacrifice, prompting her to send a destructive boar and leading to the Calydonian boar hunt, in which Meleager killed the boar and awarded its skin to Atalanta. Meleager later died after Althaea burned the brand on which his life depended, though another account says he died fighting after defending Calydon. The narrative then follows Tydeus and Diomedes, including Oeneus’s overthrow, restoration, and burial.

l: Porthaon, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Porthaon and Euryte had sons named Oeneus, Agrius, Alcathous, Melas, and Leucopaeus, and a daughter named Sterope. Sterope was said to have become the mother of the Sirens by Achelous.

l: Thestius, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Thestius had daughters named Althaea, Leda, and Hypermnestra, and sons named Iphiclus, Evippus, Plexippus, and Eurypylus by Eurythemis. His sons later claimed the boar skin, and Meleager killed them after they took it from Atalanta.

l: Althaea, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Althaea was the wife of Oeneus and the mother of Meleager. After learning that Meleager’s life depended on a burning brand, she hid it in a chest; later, grieving the deaths of her brothers, she burned it, causing Meleager to die. After her death, Oeneus married Periboea.

l: Oeneus, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Oeneus ruled Calydon and was the first to receive a vine-plant from Dionysus. He sacrificed to all the gods except Artemis, whose anger brought the destructive boar to his land, and he summoned the noblest men of Greece to hunt it. He was later deprived of his kingdom, imprisoned and tormented by the sons of Agrius, restored through Diomedes, and eventually killed by the surviving sons of Agrius; Diomedes buried him at Argos.

l: Meleager, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Meleager was the son of Oeneus and Althaea, though some said Ares was his father. He led the killing of Artemis’s boar, gave its skin to Atalanta, and killed the sons of Thestius when they took it from her. In one account Althaea’s burning of the brand caused his death; in another, he died fighting after leaving his home to defend Calydon.

l: burning brand, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: The Fates declared that Meleager would die when the burning brand on the hearth was consumed. Althaea removed the brand and kept it in a chest, but later burned it, and Meleager immediately died.

l: Artemis’s boar, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Artemis sent the boar because Oeneus had omitted her from a sacrifice. The boar was exceptionally large and strong, ruined the land, and killed cattle and people until it was hunted by the assembled heroes.

l: Calydonian boar hunt, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Oeneus organized the Calydonian boar hunt and promised the boar’s skin to whoever killed it. Atalanta first wounded the boar, Amphiaraus struck its eye, and Meleager killed it with a blow to the flank.

l: Atalanta, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Atalanta, daughter of Schoeneus, joined the hunt from Arcadia despite objections from some of the men. She was the first to strike the boar and received its skin from Meleager, but the sons of Thestius took it from her before Meleager reclaimed it and returned it to her.

l: boar skin, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: The boar skin was promised by Oeneus as the prize for killing the beast. Meleager gave it to Atalanta, but the sons of Thestius seized it, claiming it belonged to them by right of birth; Meleager killed them and restored the skin to Atalanta.

l: Tydeus, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Tydeus was born to Oeneus by Periboea, though Pisander said that his mother was Gorge. After killing relatives or conspirators against Oeneus, according to differing accounts, he was exiled and fled to Argos, where he married Deipyle and fathered Diomedes. He later marched against Thebes with Adrastus and died from a wound inflicted by Melanippus.

l: Argos, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Argos received Tydeus after his exile from Calydon, and Tydeus married Deipyle there. Diomedes later came from Argos with Alcmaeon to attack the sons of Agrius, and he brought Oeneus’s body to Argos for burial at the place called Oenoe.

l: Diomedes, The Library, rescued Ares by stealth, and Artemis killed the
s: Diomedes was the son of Tydeus and Deipyle. He came secretly from Argos with Alcmaeon, killed nearly all the sons of Agrius, gave the kingdom to Andraemon because Oeneus was old, and took Oeneus to the Peloponnese. After Oeneus was killed, Diomedes carried his body to Argos and buried it at Oenoe.

l: The Library, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Athamas rules Boeotia, has Phrixus and Helle with Nephele, and later has Learchus and Melicertes with Ino. Ino causes a famine and contrives for Phrixus to be sacrificed to Zeus, but Nephele rescues Phrixus and Helle with a golden-fleeced ram; Helle falls into the sea, while Phrixus reaches the Colchians and gives the ram’s fleece to Aeetes. Athamas later loses Learchus and Melicertes, while Sisyphus is punished in Hades and Salmoneus is destroyed by Zeus for claiming to be Zeus.

l: Athamas, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Athamas rules Boeotia and has Phrixus and Helle by Nephele, and Learchus and Melicertes by Ino. He is induced to bring Phrixus to the altar for sacrifice, but Nephele rescues him. Later, Athamas loses Learchus and Melicertes, is banished from Boeotia, and settles in a land he names Athamantia.

l: Nephele, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Nephele is the mother of Phrixus and Helle by Athamas. She rescues them from the altar and gives them a golden-fleeced ram, carrying them through the sky.

l: Phrixus, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Phrixus is Athamas and Nephele’s son and is brought to an altar to be sacrificed to Zeus. Nephele rescues him, and he reaches the Colchians, where he marries Chalciope and sacrifices the golden-fleeced ram to Zeus. He gives the ram’s fleece to Aeetes.

l: Helle, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Helle is Athamas and Nephele’s daughter. While being carried by the golden-fleeced ram over the sea between Sigeum and the Chersonese, she slips into the deep and dies.

l: Ino, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Ino is Athamas’s second wife and the mother of Learchus and Melicertes. She plots against Phrixus and Helle by persuading the women to parch the wheat, then bribes the messengers from Delphi to claim that Phrixus must be sacrificed. Later, she throws herself and Melicertes into the sea.

l: Zeus, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Zeus is the deity to whom Phrixus is said to be sacrificed and to whom Phrixus sacrifices the golden-fleeced ram. Zeus later destroys Salmoneus, his city, and its inhabitants with a thunderbolt.

l: golden-fleeced ram, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: The golden-fleeced ram is given by Nephele to Phrixus and Helle and carries them through the sky over land and sea. Phrixus sacrifices it to Zeus and gives its fleece to Aeetes.

l: Hellespont, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: The sea where Helle drowns is thereafter called the Hellespont after her.

l: Aeetes, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Aeetes rules the Colchians and receives Phrixus, giving him Chalciope as a wife. He receives the fleece of the golden-fleeced ram from Phrixus and nails it to an oak in a grove of Ares.

l: Sisyphus, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, founds Ephyra, later called Corinth, and has Glaucus by Merope. In Hades, he is punished by repeatedly rolling a stone toward the top, where it rebounds backward. He suffers this punishment after telling Asopus that Zeus had secretly carried off Aegina.

l: Salmoneus, The Library, IX. Τῶν δὲ Αἰόλον παίδων ᾿Αθάμας, Βοιωτίας
s: Salmoneus dwells first in Thessaly and later founds a city in Elis. Claiming to be Zeus, he takes Zeus’s sacrifices for himself and imitates thunder and lightning. Zeus strikes him with a thunderbolt and destroys his city and all its inhabitants.

l: The Library, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus, secretly bore twin sons, Pelias and Neleus, after Poseidon approached her in the likeness of Enipeus. The twins were exposed, rescued and raised by a horse-keeper, later recognized Tyro, and killed their stepmother Sidero; Pelias ruled in Thessaly, while Neleus founded Pylus and fathered Nestor and other children. Neleus’s daughter Pero was won for Bias after Melampus obtained the kine of Phylacus, and Melampus later settled in Argos with Bias after healing the women driven mad by Dionysus. The genealogy continues through Bias’s son Adrastus, and through Cretheus’s son Pheres to Admetus, who reigned at Pherae while Apollo served him.

l: Tyro, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice, was brought up by Cretheus and conceived a passion for the river Enipeus. Poseidon approached her in the likeness of Enipeus, and she secretly bore twin sons, Pelias and Neleus, whom she exposed. When they were grown, they recognized her and killed her stepmother Sidero, who had ill-treated her.

l: Cretheus, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Cretheus brought up Tyro, his brother Salmoneus’s daughter. He founded Iolcus and married Tyro, by whom he had Aeson, Amythaon, and Pheres.

l: Poseidon, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Poseidon approached Tyro in the likeness of the river Enipeus and fathered her twin sons, Pelias and Neleus. He granted Neleus’s son Periclymenus the power to change his shape.
